Q: Seemingly bad design choices in C++? Why are things the way they are? A:

It's rather typical for C++, but to call it a problem overstates things. A language needs to serve its functions above all, being designed nicely is a bonus.

The real issue is that an old language that aims to be backwards compatible (not perfectly but to a significant extent) will accumulate oddities like this. Imperfect design? You can only fix it by adding stuff, not changing what exists. Adding 2 things with a common set of basic features will lead to redundancy. Fix what you consider a mistake too radically? If it was used a lot, half the world will stick with the old because less work, half will switch to the new so you can't roll back, and some people won't like either. (The whole mess with exceptions.) Now you've got 2 competing designs.

Many oddities are caused by C++ being a multi-paradigm language.

If you design a "nice" language from scratch recently, you have decades of mistakes to learn from, a much more constrained scope and no flood of competing demands choking you. Let such a language live a popular and long life with updates, though, and see what it ends up as.

Q: Can I build an IdentityServer4 authentication server using Blazor Server and use it for multiple Blazor WebAssembly applications? A:

thank you for your answer!

Just to clarify my scenario a bit more:

I’m trying to understand if it’s possible to use Blazor Server as the UI layer for IdentityServer4, especially for the authentication flow (login, logout, etc.).

So instead of using the default IdentityServer UI (MVC/Razor pages), I would like to:

  • Host IdentityServer4 inside an ASP.NET Core app

  • Use Blazor Server components for the login/logout pages

  • Keep IdentityServer responsible for OAuth2 / OpenID Connect

  • Handle user authentication through ASP.NET Identity

My main question is:

Is this architecture supported or recommended in production, or are there any limitations or pitfalls when using Blazor Server for IdentityServer UI (especially regarding redirects, cookies, or OIDC flow handling)?

Also, if you have seen this approach before, would you recommend separating IdentityServer from the Blazor UI instead?

Thanks again for your help!

Q: video generation in blender using python scripts A:

I get the same error when I run it as python script.py
but code works for me when I use full Blender

blender --background --python script.py

Probably module runs blender/engine which doesn't support FFMPEG

Or maybe problem is that python script.py runs bpy 5.1.2
but with blender runs bpy 4.0.2

Blender doc: Use Blender without its User Interface

Meanwhile I found answer on site for Blender:
python - FFMPEG not available - Blender Stack Exchange

It needs to use media_type with VIDEO
instead of using file_format with FFMPEG.

#bpy.context.scene.render.image_settings.file_format = 'FFMPEG'
bpy.context.scene.render.image_settings.media_type = 'VIDEO'

and this works for me with bpy 5.1.2

Q: How to deduplicate (based on two identical columns) and merge the remaining columns into a single row for a large dataframe? A:

dplyr

dplyr::reframe(df, .by = c(ID, newdate), across(everything(), ~ na.omit(.x)[1]))
#   ID    newdate HFAdmission link_type   ADMIDATE
# 1  A       <NA>  2020-01-01    Linked       <NA>
# 2  A 2020-02-01  2020-02-01   HF only       <NA>
# 3  A 2020-03-01  2020-03-01   HF only 2020-03-01
# 4  A 2020-04-01        <NA>  HES only 2020-04-01
# 5  A 2020-05-01        <NA>  HES only 2020-05-01
# 6  B       <NA>  2020-06-01    Linked       <NA>
# 7  B 2020-07-01  2020-07-01   HF only 2020-07-01

base R

grps <- subset(df, select = c(newdate, ID)) |>
  lapply(function(.x) match(.x, unique(.x)))
aggregate(
  subset(df, select = -c(newdate, ID)), grps,
  FUN = function(.x) na.omit(.x)[1]) |>
  transform(ID = unique(df$ID)[ID], newdate = unique(df$newdate)[newdate])
#      newdate ID HFAdmission link_type   ADMIDATE
# 1       <NA>  A  2020-01-01    Linked       <NA>
# 2 2020-02-01  A  2020-02-01   HF only       <NA>
# 3 2020-03-01  A  2020-03-01   HF only 2020-03-01
# 4 2020-04-01  A        <NA>  HES only 2020-04-01
# 5 2020-05-01  A        <NA>  HES only 2020-05-01
# 6       <NA>  B  2020-06-01    Linked       <NA>
# 7 2020-07-01  B  2020-07-01   HF only 2020-07-01

We need the special handling of match(.x, unique(.x)) because by default aggregate is going to drop the groups where either of the id fields are NA (rows 1 and 7).

data.table

An alternative approach to Tobo's answer. The use of data.table may be a little more efficient than dplyr or base when working with very large data, though the fact that this process is filtering the data (changing the number of rows) means that it will not be as memory-ideal as one might hope.

library(data.table)
setDT(df)
df[, lapply(.SD, function(.x) na.omit(.x)[1]), .(ID, newdate)]
#        ID    newdate HFAdmission link_type   ADMIDATE
#    <char>     <char>      <char>    <char>     <char>
# 1:      A       <NA>  2020-01-01    Linked       <NA>
# 2:      A 2020-02-01  2020-02-01   HF only       <NA>
# 3:      A 2020-03-01  2020-03-01   HF only 2020-03-01
# 4:      A 2020-04-01        <NA>  HES only 2020-04-01
# 5:      A 2020-05-01        <NA>  HES only 2020-05-01
# 6:      B       <NA>  2020-06-01    Linked       <NA>
# 7:      B 2020-07-01  2020-07-01   HF only 2020-07-01
